1:
The date is fixed the same way by four of them, with only the arithmetic varying. Gill places it near two years after the foundation of the temple was laid and near two years before it was finished. Ellicott gives the year as 518 before Christ, the second after the rebuilding began. Clarke adds the calendar note, that the ninth month answers to part of November and December,, and observes that the month-names appear only under and after the captivity. Henry measures the interval from the prophet's earlier visions at above two years,, noting that he had not been idle in between but had preached no sermon then that was left on record.

Who sent the deputation is the chief question of the passage. Gill notes that the Hebrew is singular, when he sent,, and reports a Jewish opinion that Bethel was the name of a man sent with the others; the ancient versions he cites render it as a sending unto Bethel, meaning the city where the house of God was then building. Ellicott denies that any instance can be adduced of the word denoting the temple, and renders it that the people of Bethel sent Sherezer and Regemmelech and their men, the name standing for its inhabitants as a city's name often does. Calvin agrees that the word is nowhere used for the temple and renders accordingly, its men rather than his men, and shall we weep rather than shall I weep.

On the senders themselves they divide again. Wesley takes them for the captives who still continued in Babylon, and Clarke the same, sent to ask whether the fasts appointed at the destruction of the city were still binding. Gill will not have it: the messengers were the Jews already returned and settled in Judea, since it is to them that the answer is directed throughout the chapter. Calvin holds both ends at once, that these were Jews sent by the exiles, who though slow to come home were not despisers of God, and yet that the people of the land addressed in the reply are the inhabitants of Judea. Henry leaves the question open and observes that the answer might be directed not to the messengers only but to all the people.

Keil and Delitzsch attend to the idiom and to the standing of the men consulted. The phrase for the errand is literally to stroke the face of the Lord, an expression for affectionate entreaty; and the priests are called those belonging to the house of the Lord not, as one interpreter had argued, because they served there in the room of the firstborn, but as the persons who by their mediatorial service could obtain an answer to a question put in prayer, the mention of the prophets pointing to that sense. Ellicott would render the same phrase belonging to rather than in, and traces Sherezer to Assyrian, borne by a son of the king who besieged the city and meaning that a god may protect the king.

The fast in question was for the burning of the temple. Ellicott dates that burning to the tenth of the fifth month while noting that another record gives the seventh day, and suggests it may have been in flames for three days; he explains why this fast and no other was asked about, the rebuilding having gone so far that it was natural to ask whether the mourning should continue. Wesley glosses the separating as a withdrawal from worldly cares and designs, Ellicott as abstinence from meat and drink. Henry reads the enquiry as a readiness to continue the fast if God should so appoint, and holds that a method of religious service found beneficial ought not to be altered without mature deliberation.
4:
The reply is not made to the deputation alone. Ellicott observes that the question, though asked by a few, concerned the whole nation, so the answer is given to all, and that the reply falls into four sections, each opened by the same formula that the word of the Lord of hosts came, a testimony that the prophet spoke not of himself. Gill and Wesley take the people of the land the same way, the men of Judea who sent the messengers. Ellicott counts the seventy years exactly, from the month in which the governor left over the ruined city was killed to the month of this embassy.

A second fast is named that the enquirers had not asked about. The fast of the fifth month was for the burning of the temple, that of the seventh for the murder of that governor and the dispersion of the remnant left with him; Clarke gives the days of each and Wesley names the man who killed him. The charge against both is that they had no reference to God. Wesley puts it bluntly, that they pleased themselves in it and not him, weeping more for the inconvenience of their trouble than its sinfulness. Clarke says the same, that they deplored the loss of the temple and its riches but never humbled themselves for the iniquities that caused it.

Henry presses the repeated words hardest. That the question is doubled, whether they fasted unto him, even to him, shows the weight laid on intention: there was the carcase of the duty but none of its life and power, and to fast and not fast to God is to mock him. If fasting does not quicken prayer, increase godly sorrow and alter the course of the life, he says, it does not answer its own intention. On the eating and drinking of the next verse he offers two readings and prefers the second, the fast-days on which they took liberty with themselves, or their common meals, self being the centre where the lines of all their actions met. Gill allows either common meals or festivals; Wesley closes the point, that God was as little minded in their fasts as in their feasts.

Ellicott recasts the sentence that follows: instead of the question should ye not hear the words, he reads the statement are not these the very words, holding that no verb needs supplying. On the former prophets Clarke notes that in Jewish usage the title belongs to the historical books, the writing prophets being the latter, but judges that here the preachers before the exile are meant. The geography divides them: Clarke takes the plain for the flat country about Jericho, while Ellicott places it west of Judah. Wesley turns the verse into an argument: if such observances did not preserve the city in its prosperity they cannot profit them now that all is in ruins.

The duties then recited are, as Henry notes, not fasts and sacrifices but justice and mercy, binding by the light of nature apart from any prophet, and he ranges them under four heads: impartial judgment, compassion between neighbours, no bearing hard on the weak, and not so much as imagining evil. Gill fills out who the protected are, those with no husband and no parents to care for them, in a strange land and unable to help themselves. Clarke reads the last clause inwardly, forbidding an unfavourable opinion of another. Ellicott corrects the grammar of the received version there, which makes the pronoun a nominative where the collocation shows it objective, the sense being imagine not evil against one another. Keil and Delitzsch pause over the heading of the eighth verse and reject as strange the opinion that the naming of the prophet there means an earlier man of that name, before the captivity, whose words are reproduced.
11:
The withdrawn shoulder is read from the plough by three of them and from the ox-yoke by a fourth. Clarke takes it of a beast pulling away from under the yoke of the law, restive in the plough, and Wesley says the same. Ellicott renders it not pulled away but offered a stubborn shoulder, as an ox refusing the yoke. Henry catches a different motion in the Hebrew, which he says gives a withdrawing shoulder: they seemed to lay it to the work and then drew it back, like the son who said he would go and did not. Gill identifies the refusers as the Jews before the captivity, who gave no heed to what had been urged on them.

What the hard stone is nobody can settle. Clarke thinks the word may mean granite, the hardest stone the common people were likely to know, or the mineral of which emery is a species, and reports a scholar's view that it was used for polishing others. Ellicott takes the plain sense to be a very hard stone and traces the English word, in its modern form diamond, to a Greek adjective meaning unconquerable that was first applied to steel; the ancient Greek version, he notes, dropped the figure and rendered it that they made the heart disobedient. Henry keeps two images at once, the diamond hardest to work upon and the flint no mason can hew into shape.

Gill goes furthest. He reports the Jewish tradition that the thing meant is no stone but a creature the size of a barley corn, able to cut the hardest stones, used by the lawgiver in hewing the two tables and by the king in cutting stone for the temple, and unbreakable by iron. Out of that he draws his application: as naturalists say the adamant is softened by the blood of a goat, so the blood of Christ sprinkled on the heart softens the hardest heart, nothing else removing a hardness that grows by persistence in sin.

Henry sets the catalogue of refusals in order as one temper rather than four faults. They would not come within hearing of the prophets if they could help it, and looked another way when spoken to; they stopped their ears like the deaf adder, none being so deaf as those who make their own ear heavy; and their hardness of heart was of their own making. On the verse that follows he draws out the exchange: as they turned a deaf ear to the word in prosperity, so God turned a deaf ear to their prayers in trouble, and men who had set him at defiance cried to him when the pangs came. Ellicott is occupied there with a point of tense, the ancient Greek version having wrongly made the clause future and been obliged to put the following verbs in the future too. Keil and Delitzsch render the two verses through and describe this second word as recalling the fathers' disobedience, and its consequence, for a warning.

The scattering is read as history. Clarke refers the whirlwind to the swift victories and cruel conduct of the Chaldeans; Gill takes it for the fierceness of the wrath seen in the dispersion. Henry notices that they were scattered among nations they did not know and could expect no kindness from, and that the land was left so empty that not a man, woman or child remained, the very roads deserted; he finds a mercy hidden there, since it was kept empty against their return, though it made the judgment look the more dismal. On the last clause he and Wesley refuse to let the conquerors carry the blame: it was not so much the Chaldeans who laid the pleasant land desolate as the people themselves, and Wesley adds the two words that settle it, by their sins.
